The BirdNET ecosystem: a workflow overview

Source: vignettes/workflow.Rmd
workflow.Rmd

birdnetR is one of several BirdNET tools. This article shows how they fit together and how to hand your results from birdnetR to birdnetTools.

Overview

A typical R workflow looks like this:

  1. (Optional) Train a custom classifier in BirdNET-Analyzer and export it.
  2. Load a model in birdnetR with birdnet_load(), birdnet_load_perch() or birdnet_load_custom().
  3. Run birdnet_predict() on your audio files and save the results with birdnet_write().
  4. Read the results into birdnetTools for filtering, visualization, and validation.

For code examples, see the Get started with birdnetR article and the birdnetTools documentation.

Stage 1: Custom training (optional) with BirdNET-Analyzer

BirdNET-Analyzer is the upstream desktop and command-line application. For most users it is not required: birdnetR downloads the pre-trained BirdNET models and can run predictions out of the box.

Consider BirdNET-Analyzer when you need to:

  • train a custom species classifier on your own recordings,
  • use advanced configuration options not exposed in birdnetR,
  • run batch analyses through a graphical interface.

Custom classifiers trained in BirdNET-Analyzer can be loaded in birdnetR with birdnet_load_custom().

Stage 2: Species detection with birdnetR

birdnetR wraps the birdnet Python package and exposes two model types in R:

  • Acoustic models detect species in audio files: BirdNET+ V3.0 (the default), BirdNET V2.4, Perch v2 and custom classifiers. Load them with birdnet_load(), birdnet_load_perch() or birdnet_load_custom(), run them with birdnet_predict(), and write the results with birdnet_write(). birdnet_encode() returns embeddings instead of species.
  • Geo models estimate which species to expect at a location and week of the year. Load them with birdnet_load(type = "geo") and run them with birdnet_predict().

as.data.frame() converts any prediction object to a plain R data frame.

To process many files and save the results, see Process many files in Get started.

Stage 3: Post-processing and validation with birdnetTools

birdnetTools is a separate R package designed to work with tabular BirdNET output, the kind produced by as.data.frame() or birdnet_write() in birdnetR.

It provides functions for:

  • combining outputs from multiple files or recording sessions,
  • filtering detections by species, confidence score, date, or time of day,
  • visualizing temporal detection patterns as heatmaps,
  • running an interactive Shiny app to review and label detections,
  • calculating species-specific confidence thresholds to achieve a target precision.

birdnetTools does not call Python and has no dependency on birdnetR; it works with any BirdNET-style data frame.

Handing results to birdnetTools

birdnetR keeps the column names of the Python package: input, start_time, end_time, species_name and confidence.

birdnetTools expects a filepath column and the species name split into scientific_name and common_name. Add these columns before you pass the data on. The species name is split at its first underscore:

df <- as.data.frame(predictions)

df$filepath <- df$input
df$scientific_name <- sub("_.*", "", df$species_name)
df$common_name <- sub("^[^_]*_", "", df$species_name)

Perch v2 names are scientific names only, so for Perch output both new columns hold the scientific name.

The same works for results written to CSV files and read back with birdnetTools::birdnet_combine(). The times in CSV files are text (see Process many files).
